market.question: Will the Fed increase interest rates by 50+ bps after the July 2026 meeting?
market.rules_text:
The FED interest rates are defined in this market by the upper bound of the target federal funds range. The decisions on the target federal funds range are made by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings.

This market will resolve to the amount of basis points the upper bound of the target federal funds rate is changed by versus the level it was prior to the Federal Reserve's July 2026 meeting.

If the target federal funds rate is changed to a level not expressed in the displayed options, the change will be rounded up to the nearest 25 and will resolve to the relevant bracket. (e.g. if there's a cut/increase of 12.5 bps it will be considered to be 25 bps)

The resolution source for this market is the FOMC’s statement after its meeting scheduled for July 28-29, 2026 according to the official calendar: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm.

The level and change of the target federal funds rate is also published at the official website of the Federal Reserve at https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm.

This market may resolve as soon as the FOMC’s statement for their July meeting with relevant data is issued. If no statement is released by the end date of the next scheduled meeting, this market will resolve to the "No change" bracket.

data_availability.evidence_clause: The level and change of the target federal funds rate is also published at the official website of the Federal Reserve at https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm.
data_availability.rationale: FOMC decisions are publicly released immediately after the meeting via official press statement; data is freely available, not paywalled, and not subject to revision.

definitional_gaps.evidence_clause: If the target federal funds rate is changed to a level not expressed in the displayed options, the change will be rounded up to the nearest 25 and will resolve to the relevant bracket. (e.g. if there's a cut/increase of 12.5 bps it will be considered to be 25 bps)
definitional_gaps.rationale: The rounding rule is defined, but the binary Yes/No framing for '50+ bps' leaves a small gap: a 50 bps increase resolves Yes, but the rounding rule (round up to nearest 25) could create edge cases if an unusual increment like 37.5 bps is announced, though this is historically implausible.

all_runs.failure_scenario: The July 2026 FOMC meeting is postponed by one day due to an emergency, the statement is released on July 30 UTC after the market's end date, and the market incorrectly resolves "No" (no change) despite a 50+ bps hike being announced.
all_runs.load_bearing_clause: "If no statement is released by the end date of the next scheduled meeting, this market will resolve to the \"No change\" bracket."

resolver_discretion.evidence_clause: This market will resolve to the amount of basis points the upper bound of the target federal funds rate is changed by versus the level it was prior to the Federal Reserve's July 2026 meeting.
resolver_discretion.rationale: Resolution is a mechanical comparison of two published numbers (pre- and post-meeting upper bound), leaving almost no room for human judgment. The rounding rule further reduces discretion.

timing_edge_cases.rationale: The end date (2026-07-29T00:00:00 UTC) coincides with the last day of the July 28-29 meeting, and the FOMC statement is typically released mid-afternoon ET on the final day, which is before midnight UTC — a tight but workable window. The fallback rule handles a missing statement, though it maps to 'No change' rather than voiding, which could be contestable if the meeting is postponed.

void_conditions.rationale: If the July 2026 meeting is cancelled or postponed beyond the end date, the rules resolve to 'No change' rather than voiding — this asymmetric handling could be disputed if a postponed meeting later produces a 50+ bps hike, as traders would have been locked into a 'No' resolution.
